claim: The microtubule (MT) cytoskeleton plays an essential role in the spatio-temporal control of eukaryotic cellular organization, cytoplasmic transport, and chromosome segregation during mitosis.
source: The microtubule (MT) cytoskeleton plays an essential role in the spatio-temporal control of eukaryotic cellular organization, cytoplasmic transport, and chromosome segregation during mitosis (Desai and Mitchison, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Desai and Mitchison, 1997

claim: The organization and function of the cytoskeletal network is tightly controlled by regulating the rate and location of nucleation, as well as MT polymerization kinetics and stability.
source: The organization and function of the cytoskeletal network is tightly controlled by regulating the rate and location of nucleation, as well as MT polymerization kinetics and stability (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2015; Howard and Hyman, 2009; Teixidó-Travesa et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2015; Howard and Hyman, 2009; Teixidó-Travesa et al., 2012

claim: In most cells, MT nucleation occurs primarily at MT organizing centers such as centrosomes or spindle pole bodies and is dependent on the universally conserved γ-tubulin ring complex (γTuRC).
source: In most cells, MT nucleation occurs primarily at MT organizing centers such as centrosomes or spindle pole bodies and is dependent on the universally conserved γ-tubulin ring complex (γTuRC)(Lüders and Stearns, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lüders and Stearns, 2007

claim: In budding yeast, homologues of the grip-containing proteins (GCPs) GCP2 and GCP3 (Spc97p and Spc98p) and two copies of γ–tubulin (Tub4p) form a 300 kDa complex (γTuSC).
source: In budding yeast, homologues of the grip-containing proteins (GCPs) GCP2 and GCP3 (Spc97p and Spc98p) and two copies of γ–tubulin (Tub4p) form a 300 kDa complex (γTuSC) (Vinh et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vinh et al., 2002

claim: Spc110p, a distant pericentrin homologue, recruits the γTuSC complex to the nuclear face of the spindle pole body (SPB).
source: Spc110p, a distant pericentrin homologue, recruits this complex to the nuclear face of the spindle pole body (SPB), while Spc72p recruits it to the cytoplasmic face (Knop and Schiebel, 1997; Knop and Schiebel, 1998; Nguyen et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Knop and Schiebel, 1997; Knop and Schiebel, 1998; Nguyen et al., 1998

claim: Spc72p recruits the γTuSC complex to the cytoplasmic face of the spindle pole body.
source: Spc110p, a distant pericentrin homologue, recruits this complex to the nuclear face of the spindle pole body (SPB), while Spc72p recruits it to the cytoplasmic face (Knop and Schiebel, 1997; Knop and Schiebel, 1998; Nguyen et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Knop and Schiebel, 1997; Knop and Schiebel, 1998; Nguyen et al., 1998

claim: Both of the γ-tubulin complex receptors contain the highly conserved centrosomin motif 1 (CM1).
source: Both of the γ-tubulin complex receptors contain the highly conserved centrosomin motif 1 (CM1) (Lin et al., 2014; Zhang and Megraw, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 2014; Zhang and Megraw, 2007

claim: In yeast, the CM1 motif is required for seven identical γTuSCs to helically assemble into a γTuRC at the SPB.
source: In yeast, the CM1 motif is required for seven identical γTuSCs to helically assemble into a γTuRC at the SPB (Knop and Schiebel, 1998; Kollman et al., 2015; Lyon et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Knop and Schiebel, 1998; Kollman et al., 2015; Lyon et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 1998

claim: In metazoans and plants, the γTuRC is recruited to MT nucleation sites as a large, pre-formed ring-shaped 2.2 MDa complex.
source: In metazoans and plants, the γTuRC is recruited to MT nucleation sites as a large, pre-formed ring-shaped 2.2 MDa complex (Teixidó-Travesa et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Teixidó-Travesa et al., 2012

claim: The metazoan γTuRC is composed of 14 γ-tubulins, and a smaller number of the γ-tubulin binding proteins, GCP2-6, as well as other accessory proteins.
source: The metazoan γTuRC is composed of 14 γ-tubulins, and a smaller number of the γ-tubulin binding proteins, GCP2-6, as well as other accessory proteins.
evidence: Statement of known composition of metazoan γTuRC

claim: GCP2-6 share only ~15% homology and vary in size from 70 kDa to 210 kDa.
source: While sharing only ~15% homology and varying in size from 70 kDa to 210 kDa, GCP2-6 share a conserved core of two grip domains (Guillet et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guillet et al., 2011

claim: GCP2-6 share a conserved core of two grip domains.
source: While sharing only ~15% homology and varying in size from 70 kDa to 210 kDa, GCP2-6 share a conserved core of two grip domains (Guillet et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guillet et al., 2011

claim: The N-terminal grip1 domain drives lateral association between GCPs.
source: Structural and biochemical studies have shown that the N-terminal grip1 domain drives lateral association between GCPs, while the grip2 domain binds to γ-tubulin (Choy et al., 2009; Farache et al., 2016; Greenberg et al., 2016; Guillet et al., 2011; Kollman et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Choy et al., 2009; Farache et al., 2016; Greenberg et al., 2016; Guillet et al., 2011; Kollman et al., 2015

claim: The grip2 domain binds to γ-tubulin.
source: Structural and biochemical studies have shown that the N-terminal grip1 domain drives lateral association between GCPs, while the grip2 domain binds to γ-tubulin (Choy et al., 2009; Farache et al., 2016; Greenberg et al., 2016; Guillet et al., 2011; Kollman et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Choy et al., 2009; Farache et al., 2016; Greenberg et al., 2016; Guillet et al., 2011; Kollman et al., 2015

claim: Five copies of the GCP2/3 γTuSC are integrated into the metazoan γTuRC along with a GCP4/5 and a GCP4/6 pseudo-γTuSC as well as other accessory proteins.
source: Recent cryo-EM structures revealed that five copies of the GCP2/3 γTuSC are integrated into the metazoan γTuRC along with a GCP4/5 and a GCP4/6 pseudo-γTuSC as well as other accessory proteins (Consolati et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Murphy et al., 2001; Oegema et al., 1999; Wieczorek et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Consolati et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Murphy et al., 2001; Oegema et al., 1999; Wieczorek et al., 2020b

claim: In the human γTuRC, two copies of the CM1-containing CDK5RAP2 γTuRC nucleation activator (γTuNA) were found at the GCP2-6 interface.
source: In the human γTuRC, two copies of the CM1-containing CDK5RAP2 γTuRC nucleation activator (γTuNA) were found at the GCP2-6 interface (Wieczorek et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wieczorek et al., 2020a

claim: Wild-type (WT) yeast γTuSCs complexed with the N-terminal domain of Spc110p self-assemble into helical filaments having 6.5 γTuSCs/turn.
source: Previous moderate-resolution cryo-EM structural studies (8 Å) had shown that wild-type (WT) yeast γTuSCs complexed with the N-terminal domain of Spc110p self-assemble into helical filaments (hereafter γTuRC) having 6.5 γTuSCs/turn, thereby presenting 13 γ-tubulins to template 13-protofilament MTs (Kollman et al., 2010; Kollman et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kollman et al., 2010; Kollman et al., 2015

claim: The helical γTuRC presents 13 γ-tubulins to template 13-protofilament MTs.
source: Previous moderate-resolution cryo-EM structural studies (8 Å) had shown that wild-type (WT) yeast γTuSCs complexed with the N-terminal domain of Spc110p self-assemble into helical filaments (hereafter γTuRC) having 6.5 γTuSCs/turn, thereby presenting 13 γ-tubulins to template 13-protofilament MTs (Kollman et al., 2010; Kollman et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kollman et al., 2010; Kollman et al., 2015

claim: The γ-tubulins within each γTuSC were too far apart to correctly match the MT lattice, adopting an open conformation.
source: Although close to MT symmetry, the γ-tubulins within each γTuSC were too far apart to correctly match the MT lattice, adopting an open conformation.
evidence: Statement based on previous structural observations

claim: The relevant in vivo conformation was determined by cryo-tomography and sub-volume averaging, clearly showing a MT-matching geometry at the yeast SPB.
source: The relevant in vivo conformation was determined by cryo-tomography and sub-volume averaging, clearly showing a MT-matching geometry at the yeast SPB, suggesting that γTuRC closure might be an important regulatory step (Kollman et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kollman et al., 2015

claim: γTuRC closure might be an important regulatory step.
source: The relevant in vivo conformation was determined by cryo-tomography and sub-volume averaging, clearly showing a MT-matching geometry at the yeast SPB, suggesting that γTuRC closure might be an important regulatory step (Kollman et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on structural observations cited to Kollman et al., 2015

claim: γ-tubulin was engineered with disulfides to stabilize a closed MT-like conformation (γTuRCSS), resulting in significantly enhanced MT nucleation.
source: To validate this hypothesis, γ-tubulin was engineered with disulfides to stabilize a closed MT-like conformation (γTuRCSS), resulting in significantly enhanced MT nucleation (Kollman et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kollman et al., 2015

claim: Higher-order oligomerization of Spc110p and its binding to γTuSCs was required to overcome the intrinsically weak lateral association of γTuSCs at physiologically relevant γTuSC concentrations.
source: Biochemical studies on the role of Spc110p in γTuRC assembly revealed that higher-order oligomerization of Spc110p and its binding to γTuSCs was required to overcome the intrinsically weak lateral association of γTuSCs at physiologically relevant γTuSC concentrations (Kollman et al., 2010; Kollman et al., 2015; Lyon et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kollman et al., 2010; Kollman et al., 2015; Lyon et al., 2016

claim: Deletion of Spc110p residues 1–111 (Spc110p1-111) was lethal in vivo but only slightly compromised γTuRC assembly in vitro.
source: Deletion studies identified that independent of oligomerization removal of Spc110p residues 1–111 (Spc110p1-111) was lethal in vivo but only slightly compromised γTuRC assembly in vitro, perhaps suggesting an essential regulatory function.
evidence: Statement of experimental results from deletion studies

claim: Deletion of the centrosomin motif 1 (CM1, Spc110p117-146) abolished γTuRC assembly in vitro.
source: By contrast, deletion of the subsequent centrosomin motif 1 (CM1, Spc110p117-146) additionally abolished γTuRC assembly in vitro (Figure 1A).
evidence: Statement of experimental results shown in Figure 1A

claim: All the components of the γTuSC, as well as Spc110p and Spc72p, are phosphorylated at multiple sites in a cell-cycle-dependent manner.
source: Supporting the need for precise regulation of γTuRC assembly and function, all the components of the γTuSC, as well as Spc110p and Spc72p, are phosphorylated at multiple sites in a cell-cycle-dependent manner (Fong et al., 2018; Keck et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fong et al., 2018; Keck et al., 2011

claim: Mutations at several phosphorylation sites have been shown to impact cellular viability, spindle morphology, or affect γTuRC assembly.
source: Mutations at several of these phosphorylation sites have been shown to impact cellular viability, spindle morphology, or shown to affect γTuRC assembly (Fong et al., 2018; Huisman et al., 2007; Keck et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014; Lyon et al., 2016; Peng et al., 2015; Vogel et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fong et al., 2018; Huisman et al., 2007; Keck et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014; Lyon et al., 2016; Peng et al., 2015; Vogel et al., 2001

claim: A significant number of crosslinks were observed between the N-terminal portions of Spc97p and Spc110pNCC.
source: We observed a significant number of crosslinks between the N-terminal portions of Spc97p and Spc110pNCC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental crosslinking mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The Spc110pNCC region and not CM1 was responsible for the coiled-coil-γTuSC interaction apparent in the cryo-EM map.
source: Thus, this region and not CM1 was responsible for the coiled-coil-γTuSC interaction apparent in the cryo-EM map.
evidence: Inference from crosslinking data and cryo-EM observations

claim: CM1 binds at a cleft that spans two adjacent γTuSCs.
source: As shown below, CM1 instead binds at a cleft that spans two adjacent γTuSCs.
evidence: Statement referring to structural data presented later in the manuscript

claim: An N-terminal fusion of Spc110p164-207 with a domain from Xrcc4 produced high yields of soluble protein.
source: Using the proven strategy of fusing weakly interacting coiled-coils with stabilizing domains (Andreas et al., 2017; Frye et al., 2010; Klenchin et al., 2011), we found that an N-terminal fusion of Spc110p164-207 with a domain from Xrcc4 produced high yields of soluble protein.
evidence: Experimental result from protein expression studies

claim: The Xrcc4-Spc110p164-207 construct crystallized in a variety of conditions and diffracted to 2.1 Å.
source: The Xrcc4-Spc110p164-207 construct crystallized in a variety of conditions, diffracted to 2.1 Å, and enabled phases to be obtained by molecular replacement using Xrcc4 as a search model.
evidence: Experimental crystallography data

claim: The electron density map was consistent with a coiled-coil, with interpretable density for Spc110p164-203 residues.
source: As expected, the electron density map was consistent with a coiled-coil, with interpretable density for Spc110p164-203 residues (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Crystallographic data shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1

claim: When the coiled-coil was docked into the 6.9 Å cryo-EM map using cross-correlation in Chimera, the X-ray model occupied most of the alpha-helical cryo-EM density.
source: When the coiled-coil was docked into the 6.9 Å cryo-EM map using cross-correlation in Chimera (Pettersen et al., 2004), the X-ray model occupied most of the alpha-helical cryo-EM density.
evidence: Computational docking result using Chimera software

claim: In the docked conformation the majority of the unique crosslinks were satisfied.
source: Importantly in the docked conformation the majority of the unique crosslinks (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) were satisfied.
evidence: Analysis of crosslink satisfaction shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: Approximately 3000 good-scoring models were obtained satisfying the crosslinks and stereochemistry for a single γTuSC bound to an Spc110p1-220 dimer.
source: Using a combination of the previous cryo-EM-based γTuSC pseudoatomic model (Greenberg et al., 2016; Kollman et al., 2015), the X-ray structure of Spc110p164-207, and representing the rest of γTuSC and Spc110p1-220 by flexible strings of beads representing the amino acid chain, approximately 3000 good-scoring models were obtained satisfying the crosslinks and stereochemistry (excluded volume and sequence connectivity).
evidence: Integrative modeling results

claim: ~98% of the models were well represented by a single cluster that satisfied >90% of the crosslinks.
source: These models were clustered based on structural similarity (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and ~98% of the models were well represented by a single cluster that satisfied >90% of the crosslinks (see Appendix 1).
evidence: Clustering analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Appendix 1

claim: Spc110p1-163 extended from the Spc110pNCC along the Spc97p-Spc98p interface towards γ-tubulin and the C-termini of Spc97p/98p.
source: Consistent with visual inspection of the crosslinks, the localization probability density map from the most occupied cluster (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) indicated that Spc110p1-163 extended from the Spc110pNCC along the Spc97p-Spc98p interface towards γ-tubulin and the C-termini of Spc97p/98p.
evidence: Integrative modeling result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: The predicted path spans from the N-terminus of Spc97p of one γTuSC before proceeding towards the Spc98p from the adjacent γTuSC and binding in the space between the two γTuSCs.
source: By considering adjacent γTuSCs, the predicted path spans from the N-terminus of Spc97p of one γTuSC before proceeding towards the Spc98p from the adjacent γTuSC and binding in the space between the two γTuSCs.
evidence: Integrative modeling result for two adjacent γTuSCs

claim: The resulting reconstructions were at a resolution of 3.6 Å and 3.0 Å for the γTuRCWT and γTuRCSS filaments, respectively.
source: The resulting reconstructions were at a resolution of 3.6 Å and 3.0 Å for the γTuRCWT and γTuRCSS filaments, respectively (Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Cryo-EM reconstruction resolutions shown in Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3, Supplementary file 2

claim: 712 a.a. of Spc97p (87%) were built.
source: Overall, we were able to build 712 a.a. of Spc97p (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A) (87%) 674 a.a. of Spc98p (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) (80%), 453 a.a. of γ-tubulin (96%), and 95 a.a. of Spc110p1-220 (43%).
evidence: Model building results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A

claim: 674 a.a. of Spc98p (80%) were built.
source: Overall, we were able to build 712 a.a. of Spc97p (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A) (87%) 674 a.a. of Spc98p (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) (80%), 453 a.a. of γ-tubulin (96%), and 95 a.a. of Spc110p1-220 (43%).
evidence: Model building results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B

claim: 453 a.a. of γ-tubulin (96%) were built.
source: Overall, we were able to build 712 a.a. of Spc97p (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A) (87%) 674 a.a. of Spc98p (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) (80%), 453 a.a. of γ-tubulin (96%), and 95 a.a. of Spc110p1-220 (43%).
evidence: Model building results

claim: 95 a.a. of Spc110p1-220 (43%) were built.
source: Overall, we were able to build 712 a.a. of Spc97p (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A) (87%) 674 a.a. of Spc98p (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) (80%), 453 a.a. of γ-tubulin (96%), and 95 a.a. of Spc110p1-220 (43%).
evidence: Model building results

claim: In assembled γ-tubulin, γ-tubulin H6 adopts an intermediate conformation between the bent and straight conformations.
source: In the assembled state, γ-tubulin H6 adopts what appears to be an intermediate conformation between the bent and straight conformations, while the C-terminal portion of the γ-tubulinH6-H7 loop that most defines the interface with the incoming α-tubulin adopts a conformation similar to a straight yeast β-tubulin, likely potentiating MT formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Structural observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A

claim: The C-terminal portion of the γ-tubulinH6-H7 loop adopts a conformation similar to a straight yeast β-tubulin, likely potentiating MT formation.
source: In the assembled state, γ-tubulin H6 adopts what appears to be an intermediate conformation between the bent and straight conformations, while the C-terminal portion of the γ-tubulinH6-H7 loop that most defines the interface with the incoming α-tubulin adopts a conformation similar to a straight yeast β-tubulin, likely potentiating MT formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Structural observation and inference shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A

claim: The γ-tubulinT7 loop in assembled γ-tubulin moves such that it now more closely resembles the β-tubulinT7 loop of an assembled β-tubulin.
source: The γ-tubulinT7 loop in assembled γ-tubulin moves such that it now more closely resembles the β-tubulinT7 loop of an assembled β-tubulin (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: Structural observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B

claim: Assembly of yeast γ-tubulin into a γTuSC may help promote a more MT-like γ-tubulin plus end conformation, facilitating nucleation.
source: These results suggest that although subtle, assembly of yeast γ-tubulin into a γTuSC may help promote a more MT-like γ-tubulin plus end conformation, facilitating nucleation.
evidence: Inference from structural observations

claim: Spc97p1-54,81-89 and Spc98p163-179 contribute an additional ~3600 Å2 of buried surface area to the N-terminal interface.
source: Of the residues newly modeled, Spc97p1-54,81-89 and Spc98p163-179 contribute an additional ~3600 Å2 of buried surface area to the N-terminal interface.
evidence: Surface area calculation from structural model

claim: A previously unmodeled 33-residue insertion in the middle of Spc98p (Spc98p672-704) folds into a pair of strands, contributing an additional ~1900 Å2 of surface area.
source: In addition, a previously unmodeled 33-residue insertion in the middle of Spc98p (Spc98p672-704), between helices Spc98pH23 and Spc98pH24, folds into a pair of strands, contributing an additional ~1900 Å2 of surface area.
evidence: Structural observation and surface area calculation

claim: A very large part of intra-γTuSC stabilization (~5400 out of ~8000 Å2, total interface) arises from sequences in Spc97p and Spc98p not present in GCP4.
source: Thus, while the much shorter GCP4 structure, which formed the basis of previous modeling efforts, suggested well-conserved N-terminal interactions, it is clear that a very large part of intra-γTuSC stabilization (~5400 out of ~8000 Å2, total interface) arises from sequences in Spc97p and Spc98p not present in GCP4, suggestive of very tight binding.
evidence: Surface area calculation and comparison with GCP4

claim: The inter-γTuSC interface is much more limited in scope (total surface area ~2900 Å2).
source: In contrast, the inter-γTuSC interface is much more limited in scope (total surface area ~2900 Å2).
evidence: Surface area calculation from structural model

claim: The limited inter-γTuSC interface explains why γTuSCs fail to assemble under physiological concentrations (Kd ~2 µM).
source: The limited inter-γTuSC interface explains why γTuSCs fail to assemble under physiological concentrations (Kd ~2 µM), and thus must rely on a combination of CM1 interactions (see below) and avidity effects provided by Spc110p oligomerization (Lyon et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference from structural data and citation to Lyon et al., 2016

claim: The difference map revealed clear density extending from the NCC to a helical density that spans the inter-γTuSC interface and beyond.
source: This difference map should contain density for Spc110p and any regions not included in the atomic model. Indeed, the difference map revealed clear density extending from the NCC to a helical density that spans the inter-γTuSC interface and beyond (Figure 4A).
evidence: Difference map analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: CM1117-141 was unambiguously assigned to the helical inter-γTuSC density based on side-chain features.
source: Based on the side-chain features, we were able to unambiguously assign CM1117-141 to the helical inter-γTuSC density (Figure 4B).
evidence: Structural assignment shown in Figure 4B

claim: Residues Spc110p112-206 spanning the Spc110pCM1 and Spc110pNCC were modeled.
source: While the density connecting the Spc110pCM1 helix with Spc110pNCC was at a lower resolution, we were able to model residues Spc110p112-206 spanning the Spc110pCM1 and Spc110pNCC (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: Model building result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D

claim: A pair of helix-dipole/hydrogen bond interactions augment binding of the CM1 helix with Spc98p.
source: Interestingly, a pair of helix-dipole/hydrogen bond interactions augment binding of the CM1 helix with Spc98p, with Spc98pD542 hydrogen bonding with the N-terminus of the Spc110pCM1 helix, and Spc110pK120 hydrogen bonding with the C-terminus of helix Spc98pH19 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Structural observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: The more C-terminal portion of CM1 that binds to Spc97p is better conserved than the N-terminal portion that binds to Spc98p.
source: Of note, the more C-terminal portion of CM1 that binds to Spc97p is better conserved than the N-terminal portion that binds to Spc98p (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Conservation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C

claim: The CM1 binding site on Spc97p is highly conserved.
source: In keeping with this, the CM1 binding site on Spc97p is also highly conserved (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Conservation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B

claim: The CM1 binding site on Spc98p is well conserved in Spc98p/GCP3 homologues throughout eukaryotes.
source: However, despite the limited conservation of the N-terminal portion of CM1, its binding site on Spc98p is well conserved in Spc98p/GCP3 homologues throughout eukaryotes (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), attesting to its importance.
evidence: Conservation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B

claim: Many of the interactions in the N-terminal CM1 region are via CM1 backbone contacts and are thus less dependent on the precise CM1 sequence.
source: Close inspection of the structure provides a molecular explanation: many of the interactions in this region are via CM1 backbone contacts and are thus less dependent on the precise CM1 sequence (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Structural observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: A structure of the γTuSC monomer at ~3.7 Å was obtained.
source: We were able to obtain a structure of the γTuSC monomer at ~3.7 Å, and of a γTuSC dimer at ~4.5 Å resolution (Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Cryo-EM reconstruction resolution shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3, Supplementary file 2

claim: A structure of a γTuSC dimer at ~4.5 Å resolution was obtained.
source: We were able to obtain a structure of the γTuSC monomer at ~3.7 Å, and of a γTuSC dimer at ~4.5 Å resolution (Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Cryo-EM reconstruction resolution shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3, Supplementary file 2

claim: The γTuSC dimer is formed from two γTuSCs in lateral contact using the same interface as observed in the γTuRC:Spc110p filament structures.
source: The γTuSC dimer is formed from two γTuSCs in lateral contact using the same interface as observed in the γTuRC:Spc110p filament structures, but as expected lacks density for both the Spc110pNCC and the Spc110pCM1 helix.
evidence: Structural comparison between dimer and filament structures

claim: During the transition from monomer to assembled open state, the center of mass of the γ-tubulins shifts ~13.8 Å and ~15.6 Å when bound to Spc97p and Spc98p, respectively.
source: During the transition from monomer to assembled open state (as seen in γTuRCWT), the γ-tubulins move in the same overall direction, approximately orthogonal to the plane of the Spc97p/Spc98p contact interface (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A). The center of mass of the γ-tubulins shifts ~13.8 Å and ~15.6 Å when bound to Spc97p and Spc98p, respectively, as a result of twisting the helical bundles in Spc97p and Spc98p.
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4A

claim: During the transition from the assembled open γTuRCWT to the engineered γTuRCSS closed conformation, the γ-tubulins on Spc97p and Spc98p slide past each other in roughly opposite directions, undergoing translations of ~6.9 Å and ~7.7 Å, respectively.
source: During the transition from the assembled open γTuRCWT to the engineered γTuRCSS closed conformation (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 4B), the γ-tubulins on Spc97p and Spc98p slide past each other in roughly opposite directions, undergoing translations of ~6.9 Å and ~7.7 Å, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 4B

claim: The Spc98p-bound γ-tubulin undergoes a twisting motion of ~5–6° during closure.
source: In addition, the Spc98p-bound γ-tubulin undergoes a twisting motion of ~5–6°.
evidence: Structural comparison measurement

claim: These conformational changes alter the pitch and twist of the γTuRC assemblies from ~140 Å/turn and 54.5° in the open state to ~132 Å/turn and 55.1° in the closed state.
source: Overall, these conformational changes alter the pitch and twist of the γTuRC assemblies from ~140 Å/turn and 54.5o in the open state to ~132 Å/turn and 55.1o in the closed state (Figure 5A, B, D, E).
evidence: Structural measurements shown in Figure 5A, B, D, E

claim: Within each γTuRC there are only six complete CM1 binding sites, the last one being interrupted at the end of the ring.
source: This reveals that within each γTuRC there are only six complete CM1 binding sites, the last one being interrupted at the end of the ring.
evidence: Structural observation from γTuRC model

claim: Only six Spc110p molecules need to be bound to a γTuRC in vivo to stabilize the full ring.
source: This in turn suggests that only six Spc110p molecules need to be bound to a γTuRC in vivo to stabilize the full ring.
evidence: Inference from structural observation of CM1 binding sites

claim: The geometry is such that the Spc110pNCC binding site most proximal to the SPB would be empty.
source: The geometry is such that the Spc110pNCC binding site most proximal to the SPB would be empty (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: Structural observation shown in Figure 5E, F

claim: A closed state is populated in the γTuRCWT data.
source: Finally, by local 3D classification we observed that a closed state is populated in our γTuRCWT data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: 3D classification result shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2

claim: The WT closed state can occur spontaneously and is sampled in the open population.
source: The fact that the WT closed state can occur spontaneously and is sampled in our open population suggests that, in the presence of Spc110p, the energy differences between the open and closed states are not large.
evidence: Inference from observation of closed state in WT data

claim: Phosphorylation at the majority of the mapped sites would seem to destabilize the assembled γTuRC.
source: Surprisingly, phosphorylation at the majority of the mapped sites would seem to destabilize the assembled γTuRC and thus may help keep unassembled or partially assembled components inactive.
evidence: Inference from mapping phosphorylation sites onto structure

claim: Phosphorylation at two sites would likely stabilize assembly.
source: Phosphorylation at two sites would likely stabilize assembly, indicating the complex modulatory role played by phosphorylation.
evidence: Inference from structural analysis of phosphorylation sites

claim: Phosphorylation at Spc110pT182 and Spc97pS84 would likely negatively impact Spc110p binding.
source: Phosphorylation at two of these sites (Spc110pT182 and Spc97pS84) would likely negatively impact Spc110p binding, whereas Spc97pT88 is adjacent to a positively charged patch; phosphorylation at this site would likely promote Spc110p binding.
evidence: Inference from structural analysis of phosphorylation sites

claim: Phosphorylation at Spc97pT88 would likely promote Spc110p binding.
source: Phosphorylation at two of these sites (Spc110pT182 and Spc97pS84) would likely negatively impact Spc110p binding, whereas Spc97pT88 is adjacent to a positively charged patch; phosphorylation at this site would likely promote Spc110p binding.
evidence: Inference from structural analysis of phosphorylation sites

claim: Mutation of Spc97pS130 exhibited a temperature-sensitive phenotype.
source: Mutation of Spc97pS130 exhibited a temperature-sensitive phenotype, and the Spc97pS208A/S209A, Spc97pS208D/S209D double mutants were lethal, consistent with phosphorylation of this region potentially having a regulatory role (Fong et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fong et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2011

claim: The Spc97pS208A/S209A, Spc97pS208D/S209D double mutants were lethal.
source: Mutation of Spc97pS130 exhibited a temperature-sensitive phenotype, and the Spc97pS208A/S209A, Spc97pS208D/S209D double mutants were lethal, consistent with phosphorylation of this region potentially having a regulatory role (Fong et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fong et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2011

claim: γ-tubulinS71 localizes near the γ-tubulin:α-tubulin interface, likely decreasing binding affinity.
source: Finally, γ-tubulinS71 localizes near the γ-tubulin:α-tubulin interface, likely decreasing binding affinity, and perhaps even interfering with GTP binding.
evidence: Inference from structural location of phosphorylation site

claim: γ-tubulinS71 and γ-tubulinS74 mutants (A or D) both exhibit phenotypes.
source: γ-tubulinS71 and γ-tubulinS74 mutants (A or D) both exhibit phenotypes, likely reflecting the importance of proper hydrogen bonding near the γ-tubulin GTP binding site (Figure 6D).
evidence: Statement of mutant phenotypes shown in Figure 6D

claim: The authors assign CM1 to the helical density at the interface between GCP2 and GCP6 in the human γTuRC structure.
source: The authors assign CM1 to the helical density at the interface between GCP2 and GCP6 (Wieczorek et al., 2020a; Wieczorek et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wieczorek et al., 2020a; Wieczorek et al., 2020b

claim: The human γTuRC GCP2-GCP6 interface is precisely equivalent to the yeast CM1 helix at the Spc98p-Spc97p interface.
source: This is precisely equivalent to our assigned yeast CM1 helix at the Spc98p-Spc97p interface (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: When the human γTuNA-bound map is filtered to low resolution, density similar to that observed in the yeast γTuRCss difference map continues from the N-terminus of the CM1 helix along the surface of GCP6 towards GCP4.
source: Furthermore, when the human γTuNA-bound map is filtered to low resolution, density similar to that observed in our yeast γTuRCss difference map continues from the N-terminus of the CM1 helix along the surface of GCP6 towards GCP4 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Density map comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C

claim: The γ-tubulins in the metazoan γTuRC structures are displaced up to ~46 Å from their ideal MT-like positions.
source: The γ-tubulins in the metazoan γTuRC structures are displaced up to ~46 Å from their ideal MT-like positions, as opposed to the 9 Å observed in our closed yeast γTuRCss structure, suggesting that the metazoan γTuRCs may be even more strongly dependent upon additional factors or post-translational modifications (PTMs) to achieve an active conformation than the yeast γTuRCs.
evidence: Structural measurement and comparison

claim: The metazoan γTuRCs may be even more strongly dependent upon additional factors or post-translational modifications (PTMs) to achieve an active conformation than the yeast γTuRCs.
source: The γ-tubulins in the metazoan γTuRC structures are displaced up to ~46 Å from their ideal MT-like positions, as opposed to the 9 Å observed in our closed yeast γTuRCss structure, suggesting that the metazoan γTuRCs may be even more strongly dependent upon additional factors or post-translational modifications (PTMs) to achieve an active conformation than the yeast γTuRCs.
evidence: Inference from structural comparison

claim: During the 'transition' from a CM1-absent γTuRC (Xenopus) to a CM1-present (human) γTuRC, the GCP6-bound γ-tubulin moves by ~10 Å to better match the position observed in the closed TuRCss structure.
source: That is, during the 'transition' from a CM1-absent γTuRC (Xenopus) to a CM1-present (human) γTuRC, the GCP6-bound γ-tubulin moves by ~10 Å to better match the position observed in our closed TuRCss structure (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B

claim: Binding of CM1-containing accessory proteins at other sites within the γTuRC would further optimize their conformation and MT nucleating ability.
source: From this we speculate that binding of CM1-containing accessory proteins at other sites within the γTuRC would further optimize their conformation and MT nucleating ability.
evidence: Speculation based on structural observations

claim: Within the centrosome, CM1-containing proteins are expected to be in very high local concentrations due to the highly colligative/phase condensation behavior of the pericentriolar material.
source: Within the centrosome, CM1-containing proteins are expected to be in very high local concentrations due to the highly colligative/phase condensation behavior of the pericentriolar material (Feng et al., 2017; Woodruff et al., 2015), further promoting γTuRC activation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Feng et al., 2017; Woodruff et al., 2015

claim: Having CM1 bound in the human γTuRC seems to correlate with breaking the GCP2/6 N-terminal interface.
source: In contrast to the yeast structures, having CM1 bound in the human γTuRC seems to correlate with breaking the GCP2/6 N-terminal interface (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C, D

claim: Nucleation is positively controlled by assembly of γTuSCs into an open ring mediated by Spc110p oligomers and Spc110pCM1.
source: The structures suggest that nucleation is positively controlled in at least three ways: (1) assembly of γTuSCs into an open ring mediated by Spc110p oligomers and Spc110pCM1, (2) closure of each γTuSC from an open state to a closed state to fully align the γ-tubulins to the MT lattice, and (3) phosphorylation at Spc110pT88 can support Spc110p binding and directly impact γTuRC assembly.
evidence: Inference from structural data

claim: Nucleation is positively controlled by closure of each γTuSC from an open state to a closed state to fully align the γ-tubulins to the MT lattice.
source: The structures suggest that nucleation is positively controlled in at least three ways: (1) assembly of γTuSCs into an open ring mediated by Spc110p oligomers and Spc110pCM1, (2) closure of each γTuSC from an open state to a closed state to fully align the γ-tubulins to the MT lattice, and (3) phosphorylation at Spc110pT88 can support Spc110p binding and directly impact γTuRC assembly.
evidence: Inference from structural data

claim: Nucleation is positively controlled by phosphorylation at Spc110pT88 which can support Spc110p binding and directly impact γTuRC assembly.
source: The structures suggest that nucleation is positively controlled in at least three ways: (1) assembly of γTuSCs into an open ring mediated by Spc110p oligomers and Spc110pCM1, (2) closure of each γTuSC from an open state to a closed state to fully align the γ-tubulins to the MT lattice, and (3) phosphorylation at Spc110pT88 can support Spc110p binding and directly impact γTuRC assembly.
evidence: Inference from structural data

claim: Conformational changes in γ-tubulin upon assembly into γTuSCs mimic aspects of the bent-to-straight transition in αβ-tubulin and would be expected to enhance MT nucleation.
source: Although minor, we also observe conformational changes in γ-tubulin upon assembly into γTuSCs that mimic aspects of the bent-to-straight transition in αβ-tubulin and would thus be expected to enhance MT nucleation.
evidence: Inference from structural observations

claim: Yeast γTuRC is hundreds-fold more potent at stimulating yeast tubulin polymerization than mammalian tubulin.
source: There is at least some role for sequence as we know that there is a strong species barrier such that yeast γTuRC is hundreds-fold more potent at stimulating yeast tubulin polymerization than mammalian tubulin (Kollman et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kollman et al., 2015

claim: A population of γTuRCs in the WT filaments adopts a locally closed conformation.
source: The observation that a population of γTuRCs in the WT filaments adopts a locally closed conformation indicates a small energetic barrier to a single γTuSC closing, although simultaneous closing of an entire ring is unlikely.
evidence: Observation from 3D classification data

claim: The yeast CK1δ kinase, Hrr25, is needed for proper spindle formation in vivo.
source: Indeed, we know that the yeast CK1δ kinase, Hrr25, is needed for proper spindle formation in vivo and that it binds to γTuRCs and stimulates MT assembly in vitro (Peng et al., 2015), indicating that it is one such activator.
evidence: Supported by citation to Peng et al., 2015

claim: Hrr25 binds to γTuRCs and stimulates MT assembly in vitro.
source: Indeed, we know that the yeast CK1δ kinase, Hrr25, is needed for proper spindle formation in vivo and that it binds to γTuRCs and stimulates MT assembly in vitro (Peng et al., 2015), indicating that it is one such activator.
evidence: Supported by citation to Peng et al., 2015

claim: Six Spc110p dimers are symmetrically bound to the Spc42p lattice at the SPB.
source: Thus, we suggest that six Spc110p dimers are symmetrically bound to the Spc42p lattice at the SPB.
evidence: Inference from structural model and symmetry considerations

claim: Six Spc110p dimers would present the six CM1 motifs required to bind at the six complete CM1 binding sites formed within γTuRC heptamer.
source: These would thus present the six CM1 motifs required to bind at the six complete CM1 binding sites formed within γTuRC heptamer.
evidence: Inference from structural model

claim: The terminal NCC site nearest to the SPB would be left unoccupied.
source: Given the observed pattern of connectivity where Spc110p CM1 extends across the interface in the same direction as the helical rise (Figure 4A), this would leave the terminal NCC site nearest to the SPB unoccupied.
evidence: Inference from structural model shown in Figure 4A

claim: Both published γTuRC structures would require large conformational changes in pitch and rise to match MT symmetry.
source: Both of the published γTuRC structures would require large conformational changes in pitch and rise to match MT symmetry (Figure 7).
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 7

claim: The mode of interaction of the Spc110pCM1 helix with GCPs is broadly conserved.
source: This suggests that the mode of interaction of the Spc110pCM1 helix with GCPs is broadly conserved.
evidence: Inference from structural comparison between yeast and human

claim: There may be a conserved functional role for the residues N-terminal to CM1.
source: The fact that both structures have low-resolution density extending past the CM1 N-terminus towards the adjacent GCP suggests that there may also be a conserved functional role for the residues N-terminal to CM1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1BC).
evidence: Inference from density observations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1BC

claim: MT nucleation from single purified metazoan γTuRCs is a highly cooperative process, requiring ~4–7 αβ-tubulin dimers.
source: Recent work on MT nucleation from single purified metazoan γTuRCs has suggested that MT nucleation remains a highly cooperative process, requiring ~4–7 αβ-tubulin dimers (Consolati et al., 2020; Thawani et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Consolati et al., 2020; Thawani et al., 2020

claim: CDK5RAP2 has been found to stimulate MT nucleation in vitro.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, CDK5RAP2 has been found to stimulate MT nucleation in vitro (Choi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al., 2010
